title: Java Problem Solving Mastery
description: Build strong Java problem-solving foundations through input/output, test-case handling, arithmetic, conditional logic, and step-by-step logic building. Learn each idea through clear explanations, worked examples, dry runs, custom tests, and progressive practice before moving into DSA.

modules.title: Getting started
modules.description: Learn how programming judges consume input, execute your Java program, and compare exact output. Build reliable test-case and custom-input habits before solving arithmetic.

topics.title: Input and Output
topics.description: Learn input and output through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: Getting started with programming problems
pages.content:
If you are here - then you already know the basic syntax of Java.\
Let's now take it up a notch and train you to solve programming problems. Before that, let us do a quick recap of what we had learned about Java in [Learn Java Path](https://www.codechef.com/learn/java).

On CodeChef and other platforms, you will come across programming problems.
- Each programming problem has a **problem statement**
- You write a **solution code** which will solve the problem
- Your code is run, does some computation and generates **your output**
- **Your output** is compared with the **Expected output**. 
  - If they match - then your code is correct!
  - If they don't match - then there is some error in your code.

Click on **Next** to proceed!

pages.title: How to print output
pages.content:
Cool - so you learnt how to accept integer inputs.

Now let's look at how to convert input into output and display the same.

Most algorithmic programming problems will need you to generate the following types of output
- Integers or Decimal values
- Strings
- An array of integers or strings

Go ahead and try in the IDE.\
Click on **Submit** to proceed.

callout.title: What to remember
callout.text: The essential skill is to apply “Input and Output” to a new input, not simply memorize the example.

pages.title: Start with the contract
pages.content:
Before writing Java, translate the statement into four notes: what is given, what is required, what rule connects them, and what constraints apply. For example, for `A B` followed by `S`, write: read two numbers, read one token, print the same three values. This prevents a common beginner mistake—solving the right idea with the wrong input shape.

A simple habit: write `Input -> Process -> Output` above your editor. If the statement says one line, do not assume the values are necessarily stored in one line; token-based scanners can read across whitespace.

pages.title: Choosing the input method
pages.content:
For beginner-sized judge problems, `Scanner` is readable and convenient. `nextInt()` reads the next integer token, `nextLong()` reads a larger integer, `nextDouble()` reads a decimal, and `next()` reads a whitespace-delimited word. The method you choose should match the data type stated by the problem.

When a task contains a whole sentence, `next()` is not enough because it stops at spaces. That case needs `nextLine()` and a little more care around the newline left by numeric reads.

pages.title: Printing precisely
pages.content:
Online judges compare your produced output against an expected output. Extra words, missing spaces, or a different line structure can turn correct logic into a Wrong Answer. Treat the output format as part of the algorithm, not as decoration.

Compare `System.out.println(a + b);` with `System.out.println("Answer = " + (a+b));`. The second version may be human-friendly but is wrong when the judge expects only the number.

pages.title: Example and dry run
pages.content:
A dry run means executing the program on paper. Use a tiny input and track each variable after every statement. For `A=10`, `B=3`, a program that prints `A-B` and `A/B` should produce `7` and `3` because integer division discards the fractional part.

A useful trace table has columns such as `input`, `operation`, and `current value`. This makes type mistakes and precedence mistakes visible before compilation.

pages.title: Edge cases in input
pages.content:
Test more than the sample: the smallest value, zero when allowed, negative values when allowed, repeated values, and the largest legal value. For string input, test a one-character word and a numeric-looking token such as `A1`.

Do not invent constraints. Test cases should come from the actual contract. A strong beginner habit is to create one normal case, one boundary case, and one surprising-looking case.

topics.title: What are test cases?
topics.description: Learn what are test cases? through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: One input is not always one test
pages.content:
A statement may describe one case directly, or it may begin with `T`, the number of test cases. When `T` exists, your code should repeat the same computation exactly T times. Each case should start with fresh variables; state from one case must not leak into the next.

A useful mental model is a loop around the whole solution: `repeat T times -> read one case -> solve -> print one answer`.

pages.title: Fixed test cases
pages.content:
Some educational exercises intentionally provide a fixed number of values instead of an explicit `T`. The important skill is reading the contract literally. If the statement says exactly five integers, read exactly five integers.

Do not add a `T` loop to a problem that does not have `T`. A mismatched reader often causes the solution to consume the input incorrectly.

pages.title: Multiple lines inside a case
pages.content:
A test case can span several lines. For example, one case may contain `A B` followed by `C D E`. Java token-based reading treats whitespace uniformly, so you can read all five tokens without worrying about the physical line break.

What matters is the token order, not the visual layout. Still, understanding the stated line structure is useful because it tells you what belongs to each case.

pages.title: Hidden tests
pages.content:
Visible samples are demonstrations, not a complete specification. A judge can test values you never saw. Hidden tests often target boundaries, equality, negative values, zero, and combinations that expose incorrect assumptions.

A good habit is to ask: what case would make my `if` condition flip? What case is exactly equal to a threshold? What is the smallest legal input?

pages.title: Build your own test matrix
pages.content:
Create a tiny test matrix before submission: normal, minimum, maximum, boundary-equality, and adversarial-looking input. This is the simplest form of property-based thinking: choose inputs that exercise different branches of the logic.

For a threshold problem `N < 150`, test 149, 150, and 151. Those three values explain the branch boundary far better than three random examples.

topics.title: Custom input
topics.description: Learn custom input through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: What are custom inputs
pages.content:
You will usually find a  `custom inputs`  box in programming problems. \
`Custom inputs`  allow you to do the following:
- You are able to see the output generated by your code for inputs defined by you.
- Test your code with your  `sample inputs`.\
This helps you debug  **`Wrong Answers (WA)`**,  **`Runtime Errors (RE)`**  faster
- Create your own  **`test cases`**. \
In programming problems - you want to find exceptions or  `test cases`  where your code / logic can fail. \
`Custom inputs`  allow you to test your code for the same.

pages.title: Why custom input matters
pages.content:
Custom input gives you control over the exact values entering your program. That matters because one sample can only demonstrate one path through your logic. The purpose of custom testing is not to find a prettier example; it is to find a case that challenges an assumption.

Start with a case that is almost identical to the sample, then change one feature: make the value zero, cross a threshold, create equality, or use a negative input.

pages.title: Run versus Submit
pages.content:
Running custom input answers: “What does my current code do for this input?” Submission answers: “Does the judge accept the code against the complete test suite?” Use Run to inspect behavior and Submit to obtain the judge verdict.

A program can produce the expected sample output and still fail hidden tests. That is not evidence that the sample is useless; it simply means the tested input set is too small.

pages.title: Turn a failure into a question
pages.content:
When a result is wrong, avoid changing lines randomly. Convert the failure into a concrete question: Did I read the input correctly? Did I interpret the condition correctly? Did I use integer or decimal arithmetic? Did I print the exact requested format?

This debugging sequence narrows the search space and avoids “patching” symptoms.

pages.title: Minimal failing input
pages.content:
The best debugging case is often the smallest input that still exposes the error. A one-line counterexample is easier to trace than a huge random input. Once the bug is isolated, keep the test in your personal regression list.

For a range condition `X <= Y <= X+200`, values `Y=X-1`, `Y=X`, and `Y=X+200` form a compact test set.

pages.title: Build a regression habit
pages.content:
Every bug you fix can become a future test. After correcting a condition, re-run the sample, the failing case, and one neighboring boundary. This turns debugging into a repeatable process instead of a one-time rescue.

Keep a small mental checklist: sample -> boundary -> opposite branch -> extreme legal value.

pages.content:
Most beginner judge errors come from one of four sources: the input was misunderstood, the condition was translated incorrectly, the arithmetic used the wrong type/operator, or the output format was wrong. A fast pre-code review should explicitly check all four.

Think of the statement as a contract. Your Java program is correct only when both computation and I/O follow that contract.

pages.content:
Learn to distinguish `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, and `==`. The difference is often exactly one test case. For example, “at least 10” means `>= 10`, while “greater than 10” means `> 10`.

Translate words directly before coding: at least -> `>=`, at most -> `<=`, strictly greater -> `>`, exactly -> `==`.

pages.title: Quick review: arithmetic
pages.content:
Java applies integer division when both operands are integers. `10/6` is `1`, while `10.0/6` retains the fractional part. This is one of the most common first-course mistakes.

Choose the numeric type from the output requirement, not from habit. If the statement asks for an exact decimal quotient, make at least one operand a `double`.

nextLine() only after every numeric read
nextInt()

questions.question: What should you do when a custom test exposes a failure?

Only reread the Java syntax.
Only run the sample once.

topics.description: Learn addition and multiplication through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: From words to a formula
pages.content:
Many beginner problems are not algorithmically difficult; the challenge is translating the story into arithmetic. If one week costs `Y` and there are `X` weeks, the total is `X*Y`. If one burger needs one bun and one patty, the number of complete burgers is `min(buns, patties)`.

Underline repeated quantities in the statement. Repetition usually becomes multiplication.

callout.title: Key concept

pages.title: Units as a debugging tool
pages.content:
Dimensional thinking is surprisingly useful in simple code. If `X` means weeks and `Y` means dollars per week, `X*Y` gives dollars. Adding incompatible quantities often signals a formula mistake.

Write the units beside your variables during a dry run: weeks × dollars/week = dollars.

pages.title: When min() solves a resource problem
pages.content:
A resource-limiting problem asks how many complete items can be produced from several ingredient counts. When every item consumes one unit of each ingredient, the answer is the smallest available count.

For `A` patties and `B` buns, `Math.min(A,B)` works because the scarcer resource limits production.

pages.title: Use long deliberately
pages.content:
Multiplication can grow much faster than its inputs. Even when the input fits inside an `int`, the product may not. Using `long` for totals is a safe beginner default for arithmetic-heavy judge tasks.

Do not wait for a hidden test to expose integer overflow. Inspect the largest possible product from the constraints.

The goal is not to write the longest program. The goal is to encode the rule clearly and completely.

topics.title: Subtraction and division
topics.description: Learn subtraction and division through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: Difference is directional
pages.content:
Subtraction is not commutative: `A-B` and `B-A` can have different signs. Read the statement carefully to keep the required order.

When a task asks for the absolute difference, order stops mattering because `|A-B| = |B-A|`.

pages.title: Integer division
pages.content:
When both operands are integral types, Java performs integer division. The fractional part is discarded toward zero. `10/6` is `1`; `-10/6` is `-1`.

This behavior is useful for counting complete groups, such as “how many full 30-minute games fit into N minutes.”

pages.title: Decimal division
pages.content:
To preserve the fractional part, use a floating-point operand. `(double)a / b` is a simple way to force decimal division while still reading integers.

Choose decimal arithmetic when the problem explicitly asks for a decimal result. Do not convert everything to `double` unnecessarily.

pages.title: Division plus remainder
pages.content:
Many word problems ask for both complete groups and leftovers. The pair `N / k` and `N % k` gives exactly that decomposition: `N = k*(N/k) + (N%k)`.

This identity is a powerful self-check. Multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder; you should get back the original number.

pages.title: Guard the constraints
pages.content:
Division problems also require checking whether the divisor can be zero and whether the statement guarantees exact divisibility. Never invent a special rule that the statement does not define.

If the statement guarantees B divides A, `A/B` is safe. If it does not, you need the rule for zero or remainders before coding.

topics.description: Learn useful math functions through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: Why built-in functions help
pages.content:
A function such as `Math.min(a,b)` communicates intent immediately: we want the smaller of two values. Rewriting it as a longer `if` can work, but the built-in version is concise and reduces branching opportunities for mistakes.

Learn both the function and the underlying idea. Then you can recognize when to use a helper in a new problem.

pages.title: Absolute difference
pages.content:
`Math.abs(x)` removes the sign and returns the magnitude. It is ideal for distance, difference in scores, and “how far apart” style questions.

Do not use absolute value when direction matters. `A-B` and `|A-B|` answer different questions.

pages.title: Modulo as remainder
pages.content:
The `%` operator gives the remainder after integer division. It powers common rules: even/odd (`n%2`), divisibility (`n%k==0`), and leftover capacity.

A remainder of zero means exact divisibility. That is a statement about the remainder—not about the quotient.

pages.title: Combine small helpers
pages.content:
Simple contest problems often become one expression once you combine `min`, `max`, `abs`, and `%`. The skill is recognizing which quantity the statement asks for.

For the range of three values, compute `max(a,b,c)-min(a,b,c)`. For equal-sized resources, `min()` identifies the bottleneck.

pages.title: Review by identity
pages.content:
For every helper, keep a simple mathematical identity in mind. `abs(a-b) = abs(b-a)`, `max(a,b) >= a`, and `0 <= a%b < b` when both values are non-negative and b is positive.

Identities make excellent mental tests because they let you detect impossible outputs instantly.

pages.title: Story to equation
pages.content:
A short story becomes easier when every noun is turned into a quantity. For Burgers, patties and buns are resources. For Credits, different course categories contribute fixed weights. For Wire Frames, perimeter is the geometric quantity and X is the unit cost.

a+b+c

pages.title: A condition is a question
pages.content:
An `if` statement asks a true/false question and selects one path. The quality of your condition determines the correctness of the entire program.

Write the question in plain English first: “Is N positive?” becomes `N > 0`.

callout.title: Key concept
callout.text: The lesson is most useful when you can apply the same idea to a new input, not just repeat the example.

checkpoint.question: What is the main idea to remember from this lesson?
options: Write the question in plain English first: “Is N positive?” becomes `N > 0`.
Ignore the input contract and rely only on the sample.
Add complexity even when a direct rule is available.
Assume equality and boundaries are never tested.
checkpoint.explanation: The first option states the concept being taught; the other choices are common beginner misconceptions.

pages.learningCheckpoint: Can you explain the key idea from “A condition is a question” in one or two sentences?
pages.exampleStrategy: Start with a tiny input, predict the result, then trace the code line by line.
pages.commonTrap: Do not code from memory alone; re-check the exact statement, input contract, boundary conditions, and output format.

pages.title: Comparison words
pages.content:
Translate common words carefully: exactly -> `==`, different -> `!=`, less than -> `<`, at most -> `<=`, greater than -> `>`, at least -> `>=`. Most boundary bugs happen when the English phrase is not translated literally.

For `X <= A < Y`, write it as two comparisons joined by `&&`.

pages.title: Ordered ranges
pages.content:
A grading or classification problem is usually easiest when conditions are written from the smallest range upward. Once one branch matches, later branches do not run.

Use `else if` when categories should be mutually exclusive. Avoid separate `if` statements unless multiple outputs are genuinely allowed.

pages.title: Thresholds and exact edges
pages.content:
Always test the exact threshold. If tax applies only when income is strictly greater than 100, then 100 pays no tax and 101 pays it.

A three-value boundary test—99, 100, 101—is often enough to expose `<` vs `<=` mistakes.

pages.content:
A conditional problem can often be split into two parts: compute the required values, then evaluate the condition. Keeping these phases separate makes debugging easier.

For age limits, compute nothing extra. Just test the interval condition.

topics.title: Conditional statements part-2
topics.description: Learn conditional statements part-2 through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: AND means both
pages.content:
The `&&` operator is true only when both conditions are true. It is appropriate for phrases such as “A and B”, “between X and Y”, or “all three sections are at least 10”.

Translate the English conjunction literally before simplifying.

callout.text: The lesson is most useful when you can apply the same idea to a new input, not just repeat the example.

System.out.println(pass);

pages.title: OR means either
pages.content:
The `||` operator is true when at least one condition is true. It matches phrases such as “A or B”.

Be careful: “both” requires `&&`, while “at least one” usually means `||`.

pages.title: Build a truth table
pages.content:
For classification problems, list the four possibilities for two boolean conditions: true/true, true/false, false/true, false/false. Then map each row to the required output.

This is especially useful for the divisibility task: divisible by A, divisible by B, both, neither.

pages.title: Negation and !=
pages.content:
The `!` operator reverses a boolean. `A != B` is the direct way to express “A and B are different.” Avoid double negatives in your conditions because they are harder to audit.

Prefer the simplest expression that matches the statement.

pages.title: Condition decomposition
pages.content:
A long condition becomes easier to debug when you name the pieces. Instead of writing one dense expression, assign meaningful booleans such as `byA`, `byB`, `allSectionsValid`.

Named booleans turn a logic puzzle into a small table of facts.

pages.title: Build the predicate first
pages.content:
For many yes/no problems, first write the sentence that must be true. Example: “Chef can buy both items” becomes `budget >= priceA + priceB`.

Only after the predicate is correct should you choose `Yes` or `No` as output.

callout.title: Key concept
callout.text: The lesson is most useful when you can apply the same idea to a new input, not just repeat the example.

checkpoint.question: What is the main idea to remember from this lesson?
options: Only after the predicate is correct should you choose `Yes` or `No` as output.
Ignore the input contract and rely only on the sample.
Add complexity even when a direct rule is available.
Assume equality and boundaries are never tested.
checkpoint.explanation: The first option states the concept being taught; the other choices are common beginner misconceptions.

pages.title: Compare alternatives
pages.content:
Interior Design asks for the lower total of two options. Compute both and select the minimum. This pattern appears throughout placement tests: compare two plans, two prices, or two times.

Do not compare partial quantities when the statement asks for totals.

topics.title: Review: Conditional statements
topics.description: Learn review: conditional statements through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: Branch order matters
pages.content:
When multiple conditions overlap, the first matching branch wins. Write conditions from the most specific to the more general, or use mathematically disjoint intervals.

For classification, sketch the ranges on paper before writing `if/else if/else`.

callout.title: Key concept
callout.text: The lesson is most useful when you can apply the same idea to a new input, not just repeat the example.

pages.title: Ties are real cases
pages.content:
A comparison problem may explicitly define a tie or may guarantee that values are distinct. Never assume. In a triangle classifier, three equal sides are Equilateral, while exactly two equal sides are Isosceles.

Test equal values separately even if the sample includes only distinct values.

For a compound rule, list each requirement separately, then combine them. This prevents missing one condition or accidentally using OR where AND was required.

pages.title: Boundary sweep
pages.content:
For every numeric threshold, test just below, exactly at, and just above. For intervals, test both endpoints and one outside value.

This is faster than random testing because it targets the places where branch membership changes.

pages.title: Ready for logic building
pages.content:
Conditional mastery is the bridge to logic building. The next skill is not learning more Java syntax; it is generating examples, finding patterns, and reducing a story to a small set of facts.

When you can explain why each branch exists, you are ready to solve unfamiliar short problems.

topics.title: Logic building part-1
topics.description: Learn logic building part-1 through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: How to solve programming problems
pages.content:
In the previous modules - we solved simple programming problems that had a direct approach.\
In this module, we will cover problems that focus on logic building. Some suggestions for this module:
- Use a pen and paper to work out solutions.\
The logic / algorithm first has to be clear in your mind before you decide to code it out.
- Don't spend more than 30 minutes on any problem. While the objective is to learn - if you don't know the approach, it's best to learn the concept / review the solution.

For Beginner's level programming problems - we think the following works best
- **Step 1**: Understand the problem statement and the sample test cases
- **Step 2**: Generate examples - Create 10 input and output cases of your own
- **Step 3**: Observations / Pattern - Observe your examples to identify the logic
- **Step 4**: Plan your code - Modularise and solve sub-components of your problem
- **Step 5**: Learn - You may come across components of you logic where you don't know how to execute the code. \
In such cases, ask Google or ChatGPT or your friends and learn!
- **Step 6**: Write the code - For simpler programming problems - Java solutions will be less than 20 lines in more than 95% of the cases.
- **Step 7**: Identify edge cases - If your code still fails - try and and come up with corner cases where your code may fail

Click on **Next** to continue.

**Step 2:** Generate examples - Create additional input and output cases for each problem \
**Step 3:** Draw observations / pattern based on the examples created \

pages.title: Problem (Make Avg) - Read the problem statement
pages.content:
You are given 2 integers - $A$ and $C$.\
You need to find if there exists any $integer$ $B$ which meets the following condition
- $B$ must be an integer
- $B$ is the average of $A$ and $C$.

For each test case, output $B$. If no such integer exists, output $-1$.

callout.title: What to remember
callout.text: The essential skill is to apply “Logic building part-1” to a new input, not simply memorize the example.

pages.title: Problem (Make Avg) - Generate examples
pages.content: Now that we have understood the problem statement, let us write down a few more sample cases or examples. Review the sample input / output given in the table below.

callout.title: What to remember
callout.text: The essential skill is to apply “Logic building part-1” to a new input, not simply memorize the example.

pages.title: Problem (Make Avg) - Observations
pages.content:
What do we observe here?
- Whenever we can generate $B$, then $B$ is the $average$ of $A$ and $C$
   - If $A$ and $C$ are both odd, then we can generate $B$.
   - If $A$ and $C$ are both even, then we can generate $B$
- When can we not generate $B$?
  - If $A$ is odd and $C$ is even - or vice versa, then we cannot generate $B$ and the output is $-1$

---

Why is this the case?
- Average of $A$ and $C$ is $\frac{A+C}{2}$.
- $\frac{A+C}{2}$ will be an integer when $A + C$ is even. Else, it will not be an integer.
- Even + Even is Even.
- Odd + Odd is Even.
- Even + Odd is Odd.
- Hence, the average exists only when either both $A$ and $C$ are Even, or both Odd.

pages.title: The five-step workflow
pages.content:
Logic building starts before Java. Step 1: understand the statement. Step 2: generate examples. Step 3: write observations. Step 4: solve smaller sub-components. Step 5: combine them into the final algorithm.

The biggest improvement for beginners is delaying code. A correct algorithm written on paper is much easier to debug than a guessed program.

pages.title: Read the nouns as variables
pages.content:
In the Farm Animals problem, the numbers have meaning: X represents chicken legs per bird, Y represents duck legs per bird, and Z represents the total number of legs. The task is to decide which animal counts could produce Z.

Keep the meaning attached to the variable. Writing `X=chickenLegsPerBird` mentally is better than treating X, Y, Z as anonymous integers.

pages.title: Why divisibility?
pages.content:
If every chicken contributes X legs, a farm made only of chickens can have a total number of legs that is a multiple of X. The same reasoning applies to ducks and Y.

This is the kind of observation that generalizes: equal-size groups often lead to divisibility conditions.

A beginner might try every possible number of chickens and ducks. That is unnecessary here. Divisibility answers the question directly and in constant time.

Before writing a loop, ask whether a mathematical property decides the answer immediately.

pages.title: Movie speed-up reasoning
pages.content:
For MOVIE2X, the first Y minutes of movie content are watched at twice speed, so they consume `Y/2` minutes of real time. The remaining `X-Y` minutes are watched normally. Total = `(X-Y)+Y/2`.

The trick is separating movie duration from viewing time. The content lasts X minutes, but part of it is consumed faster.

pages.title: Complement reasoning
pages.content:
In Flip Cards, if X of N cards are face-up, then N-X are face-down. To make all cards face-up, you flip the face-down cards; to make all cards face-down, you flip the face-up cards. Therefore the minimum is `min(X,N-X)`.

Complement counts are a common shortcut. When a state has two exhaustive categories, one count determines the other.

pages.content:
A target N reached in jumps of size X often needs `ceil(N/X)`. In integer arithmetic for positive values, `ceil(N/X)` can be written `(N+X-1)/X`.

Test an exact multiple and a non-multiple: 20/5 -> 4, 7/5 -> 2.

pages.title: Coordinates and changes
pages.content:
A move between two cells can be described by row change and column change. Rather than simulating a path, inspect whether each coordinate changed.

For the reworked row/column task, both coordinates changing is one case; otherwise the alternate cost applies.

pages.title: Tiny subset enumeration
pages.content:
With only three weights, there are just seven non-empty subsets. Enumerating them is clearer than inventing a larger algorithm.

This is a useful beginner lesson: brute force is perfectly appropriate when the search space is tiny and bounded.

pages.title: Compare ratios safely
pages.content:
When two completion times are `A/X` and `B/Y`, using floating-point division is unnecessary. Compare cross-products `A*Y` and `B*X` instead.

Cross multiplication keeps the comparison exact as long as the product fits in the chosen numeric type.

pages.title: Build a score equation
pages.content:
If each correct answer adds 3 points and each incorrect answer subtracts 1, then with N total questions and X correct, incorrect = N-X and score = `3X-(N-X)`.

Convert every scoring rule into an algebraic term before writing conditions.

pages.title: Choose the right level of brute force
pages.content:
Use direct formulas when a pattern is obvious, but do not fear small enumeration when there are only a handful of possibilities. Good problem solving is about controlling complexity, not avoiding loops at all costs.

A three-item subset problem is a classic case where enumeration is easier to explain and prove.

Only when N is huge.
Never.
Only for strings.

options: It compares A/X and B/Y exactly without floating-point rounding.
It computes their sum.
It sorts the values.
It changes the denominators.

The number of test cases.

topicQuiz.question: How can room number map to a 10-room floor group?
topicQuiz.explanation: Zero-based grouping makes 1–10 map to group 0, 11–20 to group 1, etc.

options: Extra delays after complete groups of three, excluding the final level.
All levels.
Minutes per level.
The last level only.

topics.description: Learn review: logic building through explanations, worked examples, testing, and targeted practice.

pages.title: Which tool should you choose?
pages.content:
Use a direct formula when the relationship is fixed; use conditional logic when the output depends on cases; use tiny enumeration when the number of possibilities is genuinely small. This is the core decision-making skill of beginner problem solving.

Do not choose loops simply because loops are familiar. Choose the simplest model that completely captures the statement.

pages.title: State the invariant
pages.content:
An invariant is something that remains true throughout your reasoning or loop. In a running sum, the accumulator equals the sum of values already processed. In a mask enumeration, each mask represents one distinct subset.

If you can state the invariant in one sentence, your implementation becomes easier to verify.

pages.title: Validate with two views
pages.content:
Use both a mathematical check and an example check. For `ceil(N/X)`, confirm the formula algebraically and test exact/non-exact multiples. For a branch, verify the truth table and boundary values.

Different checks catch different bugs. A formula can be algebraically sound but typed incorrectly; a sample can match accidentally.

pages.title: Complexity still matters
pages.content:
Even simple problems benefit from a complexity statement. A constant-time formula is O(1); scanning N values is O(N); seven-subset enumeration is O(1) because the number 7 is fixed.

Learning to state complexity early prepares you for genuine DSA problems later.

pages.title: Explain before you submit
pages.content:
A final self-check should answer: What does each variable mean? Why does the formula/condition work? What happens at the boundaries? What is the time and space complexity?

This is how you move from “code that passes” to “code you can explain in an interview or code review.”
